title: AI careers deep dive
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this lesson, students step into the shoes of three key AI professionals — the Machine Learning (ML) Engineer, the AI Ethicist, and the Data Scientist — to understand what these people actually do day-to-day, what skills and tools they use, and how their roles connect and sometimes conflict when building real AI systems.

Rather than reading a static job description, students will use an AI chatbot as a "virtual career interviewee," asking it to role-play as each professional. They will conduct three mini-interviews, take notes, and then work in small groups to map out how these three roles would collaborate on a single real-world AI project (for example, building an app that recommends school subjects to students based on their grades). The lesson ends with each group presenting a simple "career pipeline" diagram showing who does what, and where tensions or trade-offs might arise (for example, speed vs. fairness).

By the end, students should be able to name at least three distinct AI-related careers, describe the core responsibility of each, and explain why ethics and data quality are just as important as coding skill in building trustworthy AI systems.

Tools & Resources

  • ChatGPT (free tier) — https://chat.openai.com — used for the role-play interviews. Free tier may require an account sign-in and can have usage limits or slower response times during peak hours; have a backup device ready per group.
  • Google Slides or physical flip-chart paper — for the group "career pipeline" diagrams (either digital via https://slides.google.com or hand-drawn on paper/whiteboard).
  • Printed or projected job-role reference cards — a one-page summary per career (ML Engineer, AI Ethicist, Data Scientist) prepared in advance by the facilitator, to fall back on if internet access fails.
  • Optional: AI4ALL Career profiles or similar public resources — https://ai-4-all.org — for extra real-world case studies if time allows.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Introduce the three careers briefly (2–3 minutes each): ML Engineer builds and trains the models; Data Scientist finds, cleans, and analyses the data that feeds the models; AI Ethicist checks whether the system is fair, safe, and respects people's rights.
  2. Divide students into small groups of 3–4. Assign each group a shared real-world AI project scenario, e.g., "An app that recommends which school subjects a student should focus on, based on past grades and attendance."
  3. Within each group, assign one student (or pair) to represent each career: ML Engineer, Data Scientist, AI Ethicist.
  4. Each sub-group opens ChatGPT and enters this prompt, replacing the bracketed role: "You are an experienced [ML Engineer / Data Scientist / AI Ethicist] working on a school subject recommendation app for teenagers in Nairobi. Explain in simple terms: (1) what your main job is on this project, (2) what tools or skills you use daily, (3) one challenge you might face, and (4) one question you would ask the other team members before launching the app."
  5. Students read the AI's response together and write down the four answers in their own words on a shared notes sheet or slide.
  6. Bring groups back together. Each sub-group shares their character's answers with their full group (5 minutes total per group).
  7. As a full group, students draw or type a simple "career pipeline" diagram: three boxes (Data Scientist → ML Engineer → AI Ethicist, or another order they justify) with arrows showing what each role hands off to the next, and one sticky note per box listing "what could go wrong here."
  8. Each group presents their pipeline diagram to the class in under 2 minutes, highlighting one interesting tension they discovered (e.g., the ML Engineer wants to launch fast, but the Ethicist wants more testing).
  9. Close with a whole-class discussion using the Discussion Questions below.

Example Outputs

  • Example 1 — Notes sheet: "ML Engineer: I train the model using student data to predict good subject matches. I use Python and tools like scikit-learn. Challenge: not enough data from rural schools. Question for team: Do we have data from students similar to the ones who'll use this app?"
  • Example 2 — Pipeline diagram: A hand-drawn flowchart: [Data Scientist collects & cleans grade records] → [ML Engineer builds prediction model] → [AI Ethicist checks if model is fair across genders/schools] → back to [Data Scientist to fix data gaps found]. Sticky notes read "missing data," "model favours certain subjects," "who checks fairness before launch?"
  • Example 3 — Group presentation summary: "Our AI Ethicist said she'd refuse to launch until the model was tested on students from at least three different types of schools, because the Data Scientist admitted most of the training data came from one school only."

Facilitation Tips

  • Keep the initial career introduction short and use relatable analogies (e.g., "Data Scientist is like a chef sourcing and prepping ingredients; ML Engineer is the chef cooking the dish; Ethicist is the food safety inspector").
  • Watch for groups where students pick the "easiest sounding" role (usually Data Scientist) — rotate roles if a group finishes early so everyone experiences at least two perspectives.
  • If the AI chatbot gives overly technical jargon, prompt students to ask a follow-up: "Can you explain that like I'm 13 years old?" — this is itself a good teachable moment about prompt refinement.
  • Some groups may get answers that are very similar across roles if the AI doesn't distinguish them well — use this as a discussion point: "Why might real professionals give more different answers than the AI did?"
  • Time-box the interview step strictly (10 minutes max) — the diagram and discussion are where the deeper learning happens.
  • Have printed backup role cards ready in case of internet/tool downtime, so the lesson can proceed without ChatGPT if needed.

Discussion Questions

  • What is the main difference between what a Data Scientist does and what an ML Engineer does?
  • Why might an AI Ethicist sometimes slow down a project that other team members want to launch quickly?
  • Can one person do all three jobs on a small team? What might be lost if they do?
  • In your pipeline diagram, where did you find the most disagreement or tension between roles? Why do you think that happens?
  • If you could only hire one of these three professionals for a small AI project with a limited budget, who would you choose and why?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Interview a fourth AI-related role using the same prompt structure (e.g., "AI Product Manager" or "Data Annotator") and add it to your pipeline diagram.
  • Medium: Research one real company (local or global) and identify an actual job posting for one of these three roles. Compare the real requirements to what the AI chatbot described — what did the AI get right or leave out?
  • Hard: Write a short "day in the life" diary (150–200 words) from the perspective of one role, describing a full week where a fairness problem is discovered in the recommendation app just before launch. Show how the three roles would communicate and resolve it, including at least one disagreement and how it gets settled.
